A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Miocene structural reorganization in the eastern Himalayan syntaxis resulted from a change from a foreland translation-dominated to a critical taper-dominated mode of continental collision.
the Miocene was a time of tectonic reconfiguration in the eastern Himalayan orogen, and that these changes were driven by a combination of crustal flow and hinterland stepping.

ductile deformation on the South Tibetan and Main Central detachment systems was ongoing until ca. 15 Ma in the central and eastern Himalaya, respectively, with the South Tibetan detachment active until ca. 10 Ma in the central Himalaya and ca. 5 Ma in the eastern Himalayan syntaxial bend, where the South Tibetan detachment was overprinted by more brittle faulting.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the South Tibetan detachment was not a single, coherent, top-down-to-the-south structure that propagated from west to east, but rather it was a composite system of top-down-to-the- north segments, each of which evolved differently through time.

the South Tibetan detachment was active for a much longer period in the eastern Himalayan orogen, and was a locus of significant exhumation of the Himalaya, compared to the central and western Himalaya.
the South Tibetan detachment is a complex system of multiple segments that are active for different amounts of time and that are not always top-down-to-the-same direction.
